title: Creating Factors
text:
We create factors using the factor() function. This function takes a vector of values (typically numeric or character) where each unique value represents a group and converts this input vector into a factor.
Below, we create a length-10 integer vector, x, and convert it to a factor called f1.
(x <- sample(1:3, 10, TRUE))

 [1] 2 3 3 1 3 1 1 2 1 2

(f1 <- factor(x))

 [1] 2 3 3 1 3 1 1 2 1 2
Levels: 1 2 3
Here, we create a length-10 character vector, y, and convert it to a factor called f2.
(y <- rep(c("foo", "bar"), 10))

 [1] "foo" "bar" "foo" "bar" "foo" "bar" "foo" "bar" "foo" "bar" "foo" "bar"
[13] "foo" "bar" "foo" "bar" "foo" "bar" "foo" "bar"

(f2 <- factor(y))

 [1] foo bar foo bar foo bar foo bar foo bar foo bar foo bar foo bar foo bar foo
[20] bar
Levels: bar foo
It may not seem like the factor() function did much in the examples above, but that’s far from true. Regardless of what type of input data we use to create a factor, the factor() function will always induce three consistent features in the resulting factor object.

title: Factors
text:
In statistical data analysis, we often need to represent categorical variables: data that fall into of discrete groups or levels. Typical examples include nominal variables like {“male”, “female”}, {“yes”, “no”}, or political party affiliation. In R, we use factors to represent categorical variables in our data.
An R factor is a special kind of object that encodes a categorical variable’s grouping information in a consistent way that R functions know how to handle. When we use a categorical variable as part of a statistical model or visualization, R needs to apply special processing to make the variable correctly represent groups or levels. Factors trigger this special processing, so they are particularly important for modeling and plotting functions.

title: Factors
text:
Where Factors Fit
If you’ve completed the earlier modules in this series, you already have all the background information you need to understand factors. Recall the hierarchy of data structures you’ve built up so far:

Vectors (dimensionless, same data type)
Matrices (two-dimensional, same data type)
Lists (dimensionless, mixed data types)
Data Frames (seemingly two-dimensional, mixed data types)

Factors add to this hierarchy, but not by allowing more dimensions or more heterogeneous data. Rather, factors add meaning by incorporating additional metadata in the form of levels attribute that tells R how to interpret the grouping structure represented by the factor.

text: You now know how to create factors and how they differ from atomic vectors. This page asks a different question. How do you decide when to use a factor in your own data analysis projects?

title: When to Use Factors
text:
Good Candidates for Factors

As noted above, R factors are meant to represent nominal variables. In other words, we use factors to represent unordered groups like the following.

Political party affiliation

Democrat
Republican

Nationality

Dutch
Canadian
Japanese
Kenyan
Chilean

Biological classification

Mammal
Bird
Fish
Insect

The 10 types of people

People who understand binary
Others


Factors are also appropriate representations of qualitative labels or answers to questions with fixed response sets.

A student’s exam success:

Pass
Fail

A politician’s vote for a bill

Support
Oppose
Abstain

The result of a single quiz question

Correct
Incorrect



What about Ordered Categories?
Basic R factors are not appropriate for ordinal variables. That is, qualitative variables with meaningful ordering like the following.

Responses to questionnaire items given on a Likert-type scale

Strongly Disagree
Somewhat Disagree
Somewhat Agree
Strongly Agree

Rankings (e.g., results of a race)

First
Second
Third


For this kind of ordinal data, we can use an ordered factor. To create an ordered factor, you simply specify ordered = TRUE in the factor() function.

medals <- factor(
    sample(c("bronze", "silver", "gold"), 10, TRUE),
    levels = c("bronze", "silver", "gold"),
    ordered = TRUE
)
medals

 [1] bronze bronze silver bronze gold   gold   gold   silver silver gold  
Levels: bronze < silver < gold

attributes(medals)

$levels
[1] "bronze" "silver" "gold"  

$class
[1] "ordered" "factor"

title: When to Use Factors
text:
Poor Candidates for Factors
Factors are great, but you must also be careful not to overgeneralize your use of factors. Of course, factors are never appropriate for numeric data that represent continuous quantities. However, a factor is not necessarily the right way to represent all variables that happen to take a small number of distinct values. The following examples illustrate common cases where a factor would be the wrong choice.

Low Resolution Measurements
When deciding whether or not to use a factor, you need to consider the measurement level of the hypothetical construct you’re trying to represent, not how the values look in your data. For example, your data may contain the results of an IQ test scored on a 10-point scale. Although this item can only take 10 distinct values in your dataset, you probably wouldn’t want to represent IQ with a factor. Presumably, the 10-point IQ score is meant to quantify continuously varying intelligence level. So, you’re working with a low-resolution assessment of the underlying continuous variable, not a 10-level categorical variable.


Unit Identifiers
Most datasets contain identifier columns to uniquely label observational units (e.g., participant ID, school code, timestamp). These indicator variables certainly represent some sense of “grouping” but not usually the kinds of groups that you want to include as part of you substantive analysis. So, representing unit identifies as simple character vectors or integer vectors is usually more appropriate than using a factor.


Descriptive Strings
In addition to various flavors of unit identifiers, most real-world datasets contain metadata fields like the participants’ IP addresses, software version tags, or administrative information about research sites. Likewise, many datasets contain at least some semi-structured textual data represented as character vectors (e.g., responses to open-ended questions, text scraped from websites). It almost never makes sense to directly convert these types of descriptive data into factors. There may be substantively interesting grouping information hiding in such columns, but you have to manually code the raw data into some form of systematic grouping variable before you’re ready to create any factors.

title: When to Use Factors
text:
Why This Distinction Matters
Getting this right isn’t just a matter of style. If you accidentally leave a categorical variable as plain numbers, statistical modeling functions may treat it as a continuous predictor (implying, incorrectly, that “group 2” is somehow “twice as much” as “group 1”). If you accidentally convert a genuine quantity into a factor, you’ll lose the ability to do arithmetic on it, and many modeling and plotting functions will treat it as a set of unordered categories instead of a meaningful numeric scale. Choosing the right representation up front saves you from subtle, hard-to-diagnose errors later in an analysis.

title: Special Role of Factors
text:
Factors often cause confusion for new (and not-so-new) data analysts. In particular, the print() method for factors shows the level names when printing factors. So, factors with textual level names (e.g., {“male”, “female”}) look much like character vectors when printed, and factors with numeric level names (e.g., {“0”, “1”}) look like numeric vectors.
However, factors are not character vectors, numeric vectors, nor any other type of atomic vector. Factors have their own class, factor, which tells R functions to interpret factors as encoded categorical variables.
Below, we create two potentially confusing factors.
f1 <- factor(sample(0:1, 10, TRUE))
f2 <- factor(sample(c("foo", "bar"), 10, TRUE))
When we print f1, the result looks a lot like an integer vector.
f1

 [1] 1 0 0 1 0 0 0 1 1 1
Levels: 0 1
But, of course, f1 is not an integer vector.
is.integer(f1)

[1] FALSE
Likewise, when we print f2, the result looks a lot like a character vector.
f2

 [1] foo bar bar foo foo foo foo bar foo foo
Levels: bar foo
Unsurprisingly, f2 is not a character vector.
is.character(f2)

[1] FALSE
Actually, neither f1 nor f2 are any kind of atomic vector.
is.vector(f1)

[1] FALSE

is.vector(f2)

[1] FALSE

title: Creating Factors
text:
Factor Levels
The levels attribute is one of a factor’s most useful features because they add substantive meaning. A factor’s levels name the categories represented by that factor. By default, the factor() function will use the unique values of the input vector to name the levels of the resulting factor.

levels(f1)

[1] "1" "2" "3"

levels(f2)

[1] "bar" "foo"


We can assign our own level names through the labels argument.

(z <- sample(10:11, 10, TRUE))

 [1] 11 10 11 10 10 10 11 11 11 11

(f3 <- factor(z, labels = c("Group 10", "Group 11")))

 [1] Group 11 Group 10 Group 11 Group 10 Group 10 Group 10 Group 11 Group 11
 [9] Group 11 Group 11
Levels: Group 10 Group 11

levels(f3)

[1] "Group 10" "Group 11"


If we use the table() function to cross tabulate the factor f3 and it’s input vector z, we see how the unique values of z are matched with the levels we’ve defined for f3.

table(z, f3)

    f3
z    Group 10 Group 11
  10        4        0
  11        0        6


We can also modify the levels of an existing factor.

levels(f3) <- c("g10", "g11")
levels(f3)

[1] "g10" "g11"

table(z, f3)

    f3
z    g10 g11
  10   4   0
  11   0   6



Nuances of Factor Level Mapping
Sometimes, the way that the factor() function maps level names to the values of the input vector can be a bit confusing. Consider the following example.
Predict what the following code will print.

Pay attention to the structure of the input vector and the order of the labels vector.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Explanation





If your prediction was not correct, I’m guessing you were probably expecting R to directly map the values in the labels vector to the values in the input vector and produce something like the following.


[1] yes yes no  yes yes no  yes yes no 
Levels: yes no


This discrepancy comes from an intermediate step that R sneaks in when assigning factor levels. R sorts the unique values of the input vector before mapping the level names provided by the labels argument. So, the labels c("yes", "yes" "no") are matched with the sorted input values c("bar", "baz", "foo").
You may also have expected the duplicated "yes" values in the labels vector to cause problems, but R actually uses these duplicates to do something quite useful: collapse groups. The duplicated "yes" entries in labels correspond to the input values "bar" and "baz", so R happily assigns all cases with input values "bar" or "baz" to the "yes" group.
We can use this behavior to combine groups when creating new factors or modifying the levels of existing factors.

drinks3 <-
    drinks6 <- factor(
        sample(c("coffee", "tea", "water", "juice", "beer", "wine"), 20, TRUE)
    )
levels(drinks3) <-
    c("alcoholic", "caffeinated", "boring", "caffeinated", "boring", "alcoholic")

table(drinks3, drinks6)

             drinks6
drinks3       beer coffee juice tea water wine
  alcoholic      3      0     0   0     0    5
  caffeinated    0      4     0   4     0    0
  boring         0      0     2   0     2    0

title: Creating Factors
text:
Class
Unlike atomic vectors, factors have their own class: factor.
Our example input vectors, x and y, are both atomic vectors. So, their classes are the same as their atomic data type.

class(x)

[1] "integer"

class(y)

[1] "character"


Both f1 and f2, however, are factors. So, their classes are both factor.

class(f1)

[1] "factor"

class(f2)

[1] "factor"


Actually, it would be more appropriate to say that f1 and f2 are factors because their class is factor. If you’ll forgive the aggressive anthropomorphism, we could say that an object’s class essentially defines what that object is, from R’s perspective.

R uses an object’s class to decide how to handle that object in various analyses. When we use a factor in some analysis, R recognizes the class attribute, and applies appropriate processing. For example, in the following code, we use the Species factor to define the x-axis of a boxplot. R interprets the factor as a group indicator and draws a conditional boxplot.

boxplot(Petal.Width ~ Species, data = iris)

title: Creating Factors
text:
Attributes
In addition to their class, factors have a levels attribute that stores the names of the groups represented by the factor.
Since x and y are atomic vectors, they don’t have any attributes.

attributes(x)

NULL

attributes(y)

NULL


But the factors f1 and f2 have levels and class attributes.

attributes(f1)

$levels
[1] "1" "2" "3"

$class
[1] "factor"

attributes(f2)

$levels
[1] "bar" "foo"

$class
[1] "factor"

title: Creating Factors
text:
Vector Type
Much like a matrix is just a vector with a dim attribute, a factor is just an integer vector with levels and class attributes.

Regardless of the input vector’s type, the data underlying the new factor will be an integer vector.

As you’d expect, x and y have suitable atomic types (namely, integer and character).

typeof(x)

[1] "integer"

typeof(y)

[1] "character"


But the factors f1 and f2 are both integer vectors, at their core. Factors are really just ambitious integer vectors wearing fancy clothes.

typeof(f1)

[1] "integer"

typeof(f2)

[1] "integer"








Warning



Unlike vectors and matrices, we cannot freely revert a factor to its input vector by deleting the factor-specific attributes. In all but the most specialized cases, we’ll loose information.
Since x was originally an integer vector, this process seems to work for f1.

attributes(f1) <- NULL
f1

 [1] 2 3 3 1 3 1 1 2 1 2

identical(x, f1)

[1] TRUE


But we clearly loose information if we try to naively convert f2 back to a vector.

attributes(f2) <- NULL
f2

 [1] 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 1

identical(y, f2)

[1] FALSE

title: Special Role of Factors
text:
Restrictions
Even though factors are built from integer vectors, we can’t do mathematical operations on factors. Since factors represent discrete categories, not continuous quantities, mathematical operations on factors are usually meaningless.

f1 + 1

 [1] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA

mean(f1)

[1] NA


In the examples above, the requested operations return missing values, NA, because we’re asking R to do a nonsensical calculation. So, the result cannot be meaningfully defined.
By design, treating a factor as if it were numeric produces errors and/or null results. This conservative behavior ensures that categorical data are not accidentally interpreted as numeric values, which would usually produce misleading results.

title: Special Role of Factors
text:
Features
At this point, factors may sound like more trouble than they’re worth, but that’s certainly not the case. In real-world data analysis, factors actually save you a lot of time by automatic the process of creating group codes. As we demonstrated with the conditional boxplot on the last page, R will automatically generate an appropriate set of group codes when you use a factor in your analysis. Let’s look at another very common example.
Below, we’re using the iris dataset to estimate a linear regression model.

The outcome variable, Petal.Length, is a numeric vector that contains the average lengths of the petals on 100 iris flowers.
The predictor variable, Species, is a three-level factor that records the species of each plant in the sample.

Predict how the model estimated below will be parameterized (i.e., what regression coefficients will be estimated).
If you are not familiar with linear regression, feel free to skip directly to the explanation.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Explanation





Notice that the estimated regression model contains two dummy codes, even though we only specified one predictor variable in the formula Petal.Length ~ Species. That’s the key point. Since Species is a factor, R first creates a set of dummy codes to represent the species groups, and then uses those dummy codes as the actual predictors in the regression model.
If we try to estimate the same model using a numeric representation of species, we get entirely incorrect results.

# Create an integer representation of the 'Species' variable
iris$IntegerSpecies <- as.integer(iris$Species)

# Estimate the wrong model
out <- lm(Petal.Length ~ IntegerSpecies, data = iris)
summary(out)


Call:
lm(formula = Petal.Length ~ IntegerSpecies, data = iris)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-1.303 -0.313 -0.113  0.342  1.342 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    -0.33200    0.12060  -2.753  0.00664 ** 
IntegerSpecies  2.04500    0.05582  36.632  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.5582 on 148 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9007,    Adjusted R-squared:    0.9 
F-statistic:  1342 on 1 and 148 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Since IntegerSpecies is an ordinary numeric vector, R doesn’t do anything special. So, this model quantifies species as a continuously varying attribute of the plant, not a qualitative grouping factor.
Of course, we don’t absolutely need factors, in this case. To estimate an appropriate model, without factors, we could create the dummy codes ourselves by doing something like the following.

# Create dummy codes to represent the species groups
iris$versicolor <- ifelse(iris$IntegerSpecies == 2, 1, 0)
iris$verginica <- ifelse(iris$IntegerSpecies == 3, 1, 0)

# Estimate the correct model
out <- lm(Petal.Length ~ versicolor + verginica, data = iris)
summary(out)


Call:
lm(formula = Petal.Length ~ versicolor + verginica, data = iris)

versicolor   2.79800    0.08607   32.51   <2e-16 ***

Multiple R-squared:  0.9414,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9406

Now, we’ve estimate an appropriate model, but we had to do a lot more work to get there. Clearly, the factor-based solution is our best option. Factors are a fundamental part of the R data analysis workflow, so R handles them very intelligently. Whenever you encounter qualitative variables in your analyses, do yourself a favor: use factors!









Knowledge Check




If we define f1 as f1 <- factor(1:3), what would f1 * 42 return, and why?
What are some of the practical advantages of using factors in our analyses?

title: Special Role of Factors
text:
Limitations
Even though factors are built from integer vectors, we can’t do mathematical operations on factors. Since factors represent discrete categories, not continuous quantities, mathematical operations on factors are usually meaningless.

f1 + 1

 [1] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA

mean(f1)

[1] NA


In the examples above, the requested operations return missing values, NA, because we’re asking R to do a nonsensical calculation. So, the result cannot be meaningfully defined.
By design, treating a factor as if it were numeric produces errors and/or null results. This conservative behavior ensures that categorical data are not accidentally interpreted as numeric values, which would usually produce misleading results.

title: When to Use Factors
text: What about Ordered Categories?

title: When to Use Factors
text:
Gray Areas
The choice of whether or not to use a factor is not always an obvious, black-and-white decision. Many cases, such as the following examples, fall into situationally dependent gray areas. In these kinds of situations, the focus of our analysis typically tells us whether we should use a factor or not.

Manually Coarsened Variables
Sometimes, numeric data can be “coarsened” to create qualitative groups. We’ve already used several such cases in the examples above. Typically, to “pass” an exam, the examinee’s score must exceed some threshold. In Dutch universities, that threshold would usually be a score of 5.5 on a 1-to-10 scale. So, the binary Pass/Fail factor noted above would typically be created by binning a continuous, numeric score.
\[
\begin{align}
  \mathit{Success} =
    \begin{cases}
      \mathit{Fail} & \text{if} & \mathit{Score} < 5.5\\
      \mathit{Pass} & \text{if} & \mathit{Score} \geq 5.5
    \end{cases}
\end{align}
\]
This type of manual coarsening is often used in biomedical contexts to simplify interpretation. Anytime medical guidance is presented in terms of a small set of disjoint groups, there’s a good chance that the groups were defined by categorizing an underlying continuous variable. BMI categories are one commonly encountered example. Technically, BMI can take any positive value, but many public health organizations provide guidelines for “healthy” and “unhealthy” BMIs based on discrete ranges. For example, the World Health Organization defines six levels of Nutritional Status based on the following BMI ranges.
\[
\begin{align}
  \mathit{Nutritional~Status} =
    \begin{cases}
      \mathit{Underweight}       & \text{if} &                     &      & \hspace{-14mu} \mathit{BMI} < 18.5\\
      \mathit{Healthy~Weight}    & \text{if} & 18.5 \hspace{-18mu} & \geq & \hspace{-14mu} \mathit{BMI} < 25\\
      \mathit{Overweight}        & \text{if} & 25                  & \geq & \hspace{-14mu} \mathit{BMI} < 30\\
      \mathit{Obesity~Class~I}   & \text{if} & 30                  & \geq & \hspace{-14mu} \mathit{BMI} < 35\\
      \mathit{Obesity~Class~II}  & \text{if} & 35                  & \geq & \hspace{-14mu} \mathit{BMI} < 40\\
      \mathit{Obesity~Class~III} & \text{if} & 40                  & \geq & \hspace{-14mu} \mathit{BMI}
    \end{cases}
\end{align}
\]
From the perspective of optimal statistical measurement, coarsening continuous variables in this way is often a bad idea, but that discussion falls well outside the scope of this tutorial. For our purposes, you should simply realize that you may encounter situations where the same underlying data can be represented as a numeric variable or a factor, depending on how you process those data.


Counts
A count variable records the number of discrete elements in a set—like the number of children in a family or the number of hurricanes in a year. Technically, counts are categorical variables because you can only count whole numbers of things (e.g., a family cannot include 2.75 children). However, we often want to analyze counts as numeric values. For example, it seems sensible to ask if the average number of children in Dutch families is different from the average number of children in Spanish families. In such cases, it would not be appropriate to convert the numeric count variable to a factor.
We don’t always need to analyze counts as numeric quantities, though. Sometimes, it makes more sense to represent a count as an ordered factor. For example, a questionnaire item may ask participants to report how many cigarettes they smoke each day. As posed, this question elicits count responses, but the data are often binned into discrete ordinal categories like none, a few per week, several per day, etc. Self-reported consumption rates are notoriously poor, so analyzing these questionnaire responses as numeric counts may lead to spurious precision and misleading results. We may be better off accepting the inherent noise of our measurement and purposefully coarsening the counts into appropriately low-resolution ordered factors.


Ordinal Variables
Finally, let’s consider a problem that’s somewhat complementary to the situation with counts. Ordinal variables are unambiguously categorical, and ordered factors are absolutely the correct way to represent an ordinal variable in R. So, it may surprise you to hear that ordered factors are not used very frequently in real-world analyses. Again, the main consideration is how the variables will be analyzed, not how they can be most accurately represented in the dataset. Surveys and questionnaires often include various self-reported rating scales like the following examples.

HEXACO Personality Inventory
Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire
Climate Change Anxiety Scale

These scales produce ordinal data, but the items are not meant to be analyzed independently. Rather, we’re supposed to aggregate the individual items into so-called scale scores (e.g., by averaging the responses). In such cases, we clearly cannot represent the individual items as ordered factors, since we cannot compute the mean of a set of ordered factors.
In situations where our analysis will maintain the ordinal nature of a given variable, however, it would be appropriate to represent that variable as an ordered factor. For example, we may wish to evaluate risk factors for obesity in adults. We could use a proportional odds logistic regression model wherein the Nutritional Status variable described above acts as the outcome variable, and variables quantifying risk factors act as predictors. In this analysis, we should format Nutritional Status as an ordered factor.






Practice



Consider the following four hypothetical variables.

A column recording each survey respondent’s marital status: {single, married, divorced, widowed}.
A column recording each respondent’s exact age in years.
A column recording which of 3 experimental treatment groups each participant was assigned to.
A column recording each respondent’s annual income in dollars.


 Question Solution


Explain why (or why not) a factor would be an appropriate way to represent each variable.



Factor. Marital status is a small set of unordered categories, a textbook use-case for a factor.
Not a factor. Age is a genuine quantity, you’d want to compute averages, compare magnitudes, and so on.
Factor. Treatment group assignment is exactly the kind of categorical grouping factors were designed for, especially since this variable will likely be used in a statistical model later.
Not a factor. Income is a continuous quantity, even though it might have a skewed distribution, you wouldn’t want R to prevent you from computing a mean or a sum.

title: When to Use Factors
text:
Much Ado about Nothing?
You may be wondering why we’re making such a fuss about when to use factors. Well, in practice, getting this decision right isn’t just a trivial matter of style. As you’ve seen on previous pages, if you try to analyze a nominal variable as a numeric vector, R will assume that variable represents some continuous value (implying, incorrectly, that Group 2 is somehow “twice as much” as Group 1). Accidentally converting a continuous, numeric variable into a factor creates even more obvious problems, since R won’t do any numeric calculations with that variable anymore. Furthermore, the gray area situations discussed above pose tricky, situationally dependent questions that you must answer within the context of a given project. Here, you’re not concerned about completely breaking your analysis. Rather, the choice of whether or not to use a factor directly affects the formulation of your research question and the meaning of your results.
Beyond these technical and pragmatic considerations, there’s also a deeper level of implications to consider. Statistical measurement is not nearly as anodyne and objective as we may wish it to be, particularly if your analysis involves human subjects or sociopolitical entities. Something as simple as the way we choose to operationalize some variable in our analysis can make very strong political, philosophical, or ethical statements.
For example, binary gender was, traditionally, the go-to example of a nominal variable used in statistics education. However, in recent years, the conceptualization of gender has shifted toward understanding gender as a fluid, culturally created construct. If you want to include a “gender” variable in your analysis, what operationalization will you use? If you don’t want to endorse the concept of binary gender, you could create a three-level factor by adding a “non-binary” option, but you could also fully embrace a fluid conceptualization of gender by representing gender as a continuous numeric variable. Each of these options makes an implicit statement about the definition of “gender”, and you’re implicitly endorsing that statement by choosing a particular operationalization.
Lest any sociologists or political scientists reading this start getting too smug, realize that you don’t need to analyze person-level data to encounter fraught design decisions. Suppose you need to create a “nationality” indicator for a sample of East Asian participants. Do you classify participants from Taiwan as Chinese? What if you need to create a “country” indicator for a sample from Western Asia. Do you represent Palestine as an independent country? At time of writing, both of these questions are highly contentious political issues, so you cannot naïvely defer to the consensus of the international community. You must choose, and your choice will have consequences.

For what types of variables are factors most appropriate?
What are some examples of variables that you should not represent as factors?
Why is it not always obvious when you should use a factor?
